curriculumTitle: Energy Systems and Reliability: Learning from the Texas Blackouts
subject: Integrated STEM (Physics, Engineering, Social Studies)
description: An interdisciplinary unit exploring energy production, distribution, and reliability through the lens of the Texas winter blackouts

parts.partSubtitle: Building foundational knowledge of electrical systems

units.title: Reliable Energy for Communities
units.coreIdea: Communities require reliable energy sources, and understanding energy transfer is essential for building resilient systems.
units.drivingQuestion: What can we learn about a blackout in Texas about producing reliable energy for our communities?
keyContent: The term electricity describes energy transfer that can power lights and other devices
Multiple subsystems transfer power through a community
units.navigation: Take one subsystem (in the form of a power strip) as a microcosm for the whole system
units.assessment: Formative: Initial Model to explain energy transfer

units.title: Energy Transfer Through Systems
units.coreIdea: Energy transfers from one source to multiple devices through interconnected systems like buildings and neighborhoods.
units.drivingQuestion: What structures in the system enable energy transfer from one source to multiple devices, buildings, and neighborhoods?
units.phenomenon: Dissecting a Power Strip - Circuit Analysis
keyContent: Energy will transfer from a source to a device when a circuit is formed
Plugging in a device completes a circuit from a (far off) power source
A short circuit occurs when there is a direct conductive path from energy source to the ground or to the other side of the source
units.assessment: Formative: Modeling a circuit, modeling a city

units.title: Investigating System Failures
units.coreIdea: System failures can result from broken circuits or inadequate production capacity to meet demand.
units.drivingQuestion: Could the blackouts in Texas have been caused by a broken or short-circuited circuit?
units.phenomenon: Data from blackouts in Texas - System Analysis
keyContent: Production for electricity must match demand
Cold temperatures in Texas winter probably increased demand over production
units.navigation: We know demand exceeded production. How can we prevent that in the future?
units.assessment: Summative: Analyze data on energy demand and production

units.title: Energy Source Reliability
units.coreIdea: Different energy sources have varying reliability characteristics and decision-making processes for implementation.
units.drivingQuestion: What makes an energy source reliable?
units.phenomenon: Data on different sources of energy
keyContent: The energy used to create electricity in a power plant comes from Earth's systems
Making decisions about complex defining criteria for success can be complex
units.navigation: How does a reliable source generate electricity?
units.assessment: Analysis of energy source reliability factors

parts.partSubtitle: Exploring how electrical energy is produced and transmitted

units.title: Sources of Electrical Energy
units.coreIdea: Electrical energy generation involves converting other forms of energy through various mechanisms including electromagnetic induction.
units.drivingQuestion: Where does electrical energy come from?
units.phenomenon: Generator analysis - wind, gas, and magnetic field interactions
keyContent: Power generators use loops of copper wire and powerful magnets
The motion of a magnet can generate changing fields, which can cause energy transfer at a distance (and vice versa)
When something moves the magnetic field through the wires, that can cause energy transfer into wires through changing fields
units.navigation: Initial and final models of how generators make energy. Design, construction, and testing of student generators.
units.assessment: Formative: Initial and final models of energy transfer, Design and construction of student generators

units.title: Energy Transfer in Wires
units.coreIdea: Energy transfer through wires involves electromagnetic fields and can be affected by various factors including temperature.
units.drivingQuestion: How does energy transfer in wires?
units.phenomenon: Field interactions, computer wire simulation, motor transfer demonstrations
keyContent: Electric and magnetic fields change when energy transfers into and out of their objects
Electric fields can push electrons, transferring 'electrical energy' is the energy of the electric fields of electrons transferred through electromagnetic pushes from fields
A turbine transfers energy through electric and magnetic fields to the electrons in a wire, causing fields to slosh back and forth continuously
Electrons cause the atoms of the wire material to be transferring energy from the external to the surroundings as 'heat'
units.navigation: Learn that cold temp doesn't have much of an effect on wires. Indicates that problem is a supply issue, not a transfer issue.
units.assessment: Model based on reading peer papers, computer simulator investigation, physical wire study, prediction/investigation, update design tracker, motor transfer task

units.title: Grid System Failures
units.coreIdea: Power grid failures can result from supply-demand imbalances and have disparate impacts on different communities.
units.drivingQuestion: What could have caused the disparities we saw in the blackouts in Texas?
units.phenomenon: Energy supply modeling with 'Electric City', hospital data analysis
keyContent: Power companies in Texas probably had to make decisions about who lost power in some places in order to keep the lights on in others
There is no one factor that explains why some counties in Texas lost power and others did not
units.navigation: Difficult analyzing data by county because they're so large/varied. Move on to smaller scale.
units.assessment: Model of energy transfer with low supply, students analyze CODAP data and limitations

units.title: Energy Equity and Design Solutions
units.coreIdea: Energy system design decisions affect different populations differently, requiring consideration of multiple perspectives and tradeoffs.
units.drivingQuestion: Why do design solutions affect some people differently than others?
units.phenomenon: Podcast analysis on energy equity and expert perspectives
keyContent: An imbalance of energy supply and demand was the primary cause of the blackouts in Texas in February 2021
Power outages depended on which neighborhood people lived in. Has inequitable effect on people in neighborhood with disparities
Power companies chose to keep power on in neighborhoods with 'essential' buildings
units.navigation: Home learning about tradeoffs for different types of energy sources
units.assessment: Response to podcast, case study review, exit slip

parts.partSubtitle: Creating solutions for sustainable and equitable energy access

units.title: Energy Storage and Reliability
units.coreIdea: Energy storage systems can improve grid reliability, but implementation requires considering multiple factors including economic and environmental costs.
units.drivingQuestion: How can energy storage make our systems more reliable during an energy crisis?
units.phenomenon: Battery integration models, energy facility analysis, and cost-benefit calculations
keyContent: All forms of energy production and other resource extraction have economic, social, environmental, and geopolitical costs and risks, but design solutions that store excess energy are important as we move into a renewable energy market
units.navigation: What other costs are associated with design solutions that aren't reflected in economic costs?
units.assessment: Formative: Modeling system w or w/o batteries, Formative: MATH!

units.title: Community Energy Decision-Making
units.coreIdea: Effective energy system design requires input from multiple stakeholders and consideration of diverse community needs and constraints.
units.drivingQuestion: What decisions do we need to make to design more reliable systems to meet our community's energy needs?
units.phenomenon: Stakeholder analysis, community energy planning, and decision matrices
keyContent: When designing solutions to complex problems, you have to consider constraints including cost, safety, reliability, aesthetics, and social, cultural, and environmental impacts
It's important to take input from stakeholders before making decisions
units.navigation: How do we improve the infrastructure in our community?
units.assessment: Potential Summative: Exit ticket to weigh criteria for community energy decisions

units.title: Final Design Challenge
units.coreIdea: Students synthesize learning to design and evaluate energy systems that address community needs while considering multiple constraints and stakeholder perspectives.
units.drivingQuestion: What have we figured out, and what can we carry forward?
units.phenomenon: Student-designed energy systems and community presentations
keyContent: Scientists and engineers ask questions, define problems, and gather evidence to address those problems
units.assessment: Summative: Project - Design challenge, Evaluate different energy sources & grid systems required for high function community; Summative: Sand and Mirrors Assessment

formative: Initial and final energy transfer models
summative: Energy demand and production data analysis
